project_metadata.job_description:
Hi there! 

I'm looking for a typography-focused designer to help refine—not reinvent—the wordmark for my luxury longevity brand, Vellvé.

Over the past several months, I've developed the creative direction through extensive exploration and mood boards. I'm not looking for new concepts or a completely different logo. What I need now is someone with a strong eye for typography, spacing, proportion, and detail to transform the current direction into a polished, proprietary wordmark.

The brand is inspired by the quiet luxury of Aman, Brunello Cucinelli, Fountain Life, Ingold, and high-end hospitality rather than traditional healthcare or med spas.

The current direction includes:

* A custom V system with a larger first V and smaller second V
* Warm champagne metallic accents
* Sculptural, architectural lettering
* Roman inscription influence without fashion-serif characteristics
* Uniform stroke weights
* A timeless, bespoke feel that communicates optimization, longevity, and elevated wellness

The scope would include:
• Refining the typography and letterforms
• Perfecting kerning and spacing
• Creating a production-ready vector wordmark
• Delivering AI, SVG, EPS, transparent PNGs, and black/white/metallic versions
• A version with and without the "Wellness elevated." tagline

I'll provide mood boards, reference images, and the current logo direction to build from.

Before moving forward, I'd love to see examples of luxury wordmarks or typography-focused branding you've created.

My budget is approximately $300-500.

If this sounds like a good fit, I'd love to connect.

A few additional thoughts after months of refining this direction that may help:

The biggest realization is that the signature of the brand is no longer just the accent over the É—it's the entire **V language**.

The larger opening V should be the hero of the wordmark. The smaller closing V and the É accent should all be derived from that same geometry. Together, these three elements should share identical angles, proportions, and material language. Ideally, if someone covered every other letter except the two Vs and the accent, it should still feel unmistakably like VELLVÉ.

The remaining letters should support the V rather than compete with it. The strongest direction we found was treating them as architectural objects instead of typography—quiet, sculptural, and intentional.

Some additional refinements I'd love to explore are:

• Perfecting the kerning so the word reads as one unified mark rather than "VE LL VÉ."
• Making the Ls feel more structural than typographic. We gravitated toward taller, architectural proportions with subtle custom geometry rather than decorative serifs.
• Refining the É accent so it feels like a brand signature rather than punctuation—slightly shorter, thicker, and more integrated with the V geometry.
• Exploring subtle internal reveal lines or dimensional details that create depth without feeling ornamental. The logo should feel like it could exist as a beautifully crafted brass or stone sign, where light naturally catches the details.

One important realization was that the logo became too severe when we leaned too heavily into architecture. I still want it to feel timeless and sculptural, but with a sense of warmth, vitality, and aspiration. We found that warmth came from the material expression—champagne metal, light, subtle illumination, and depth—not from softer or more decorative typography.

Please feel free to challenge the typography, but preserve the design language. I'm more interested in refining the DNA of the wordmark than introducing entirely new ideas.

Ultimately, I don't think this project is about creating a beautiful font. It's about creating a proprietary wordmark that feels inevitable—as though VELLVÉ could never have been written any other way.

If there's one thing I'd love to achieve, it's this: the opening V should eventually become recognizable enough to stand on its own as a long-term brand asset, without ever needing a separate icon or monogram. The wordmark itself should become the identity.

By focusing purely on these underlying rules, the forms feel inevitable rather than chosen.

I'd love to know which of these two structural philosophies feels right as the definitive blueprint for Vellvé.

Hi Abdulbari,

Thank you for this latest iteration. The hierarchy is moving back in the right direction, but I think we need to reset our review process so we stop taking steps backward.

From this point forward, I'd like every presentation to follow the same format.

These relationships should remain locked unless I specifically request otherwise:
Hero V — Maintain the current agreed hierarchy and percentage of elevation of the right arm. This remains the master geometry for the system.
Second V — Derived proportionally from the Hero V, maintaining the agreed relationship above the cap height of the surrounding letters. It should remain a quiet echo of the Hero V, never competing with it.
É Accent — An exact copy of the Hero V's right arm, terminating at the identical peak height and inheriting the exact same terminal geometry.
Presentation

For every future iteration, I'd like to see two versions of each option.

Left column

Hero V peak height
Alphabet cap height
Second V peak height

Right column

The identical artwork with all reference lines removed.

This allows me to evaluate the design itself while also confirming that the hierarchy remains intact.

New Assignment: Terminal Exploration

I believe the hierarchy is now close enough that I'd like to focus exclusively on the terminal language.

Please keep everything else identical and explore six distinctly different terminal treatments for the Hero V only.

I'm not looking for six refinements of the same solution. I'm looking for genuinely different design philosophies.

Here are five directions that may help guide the exploration:

1\. Soft Architectural

Think carved limestone, travertine, or high-end architecture.

Still geometric
Corners subtly eased
Warm without appearing rounded
Quiet confidence
2\. Sculpted

Imagine the termination wasn't cut.

It was carefully sculpted.

Subtle transitions
Almost invisible refinement
Hand-finished rather than manufactured
Elegant restraint
3\. Faceted Gemstone

Think of a precision-cut gemstone.

Multiple subtle planes
Refined rather than sharp
Luxurious without becoming decorative
Crisp, but polished
4\. Cast Bronze

Imagine molten bronze poured into a mold.

Geometry remains precise
Edges naturally soften through the casting process
Less mechanical
Timeless and enduring
5\. Bespoke Furniture

Think of museum-quality cabinetry or artisan furniture making.

The edge has been intentionally broken
Engineered but never harsh
Sophisticated craftsmanship
Understated luxury
6\. Your Interpretation

I'd also like one concept that is entirely your own interpretation.

Based on everything we've developed together over the past several weeks, I'd like to see where your own design intuition leads you. Surprise me with a solution that you believe best captures the VELLVÉ identity.

What I'm searching for is not a softer vector.

I'm searching for a different material quality.

The terminal should feel less like the end of a line and more like the edge treatment of an heirloom object.

It should feel:

Architectural
Refined
Quiet
Luxurious
Timeless
Precision-crafted

It should never feel:

Calligraphic
Rounded
Decorative
Fashion-oriented
Aggressive or sharp

Once we identify the right terminal language for the Hero V, it should then be applied directly to the É accent and proportionally to the second V.

Thank you.
